_note:
Replies to journal entries. Every inbound message gets one -- silence on the path where the most work was done is the thing this exists to fix.

Design rules held here: praise habituates within a week, so the strongest shapes reference evidence instead. `mechanism` names what the entry actually did, using the mechanism already stored on the entry. `streak` states a fact about who Seth is. `short` stays warm but small, because an effusive reply to a two-word entry teaches that two-word entries pay. `identity` is the always-available fallback so no path can ever be silent.

implementation_intention: You just turned an intention into a trigger. That is the whole difference between wanting and doing.
Naming when and where is the part almost everyone skips. You didn't.
identity: That's a vote for the person you're becoming. They accumulate.
You just described yourself as someone who does this. That sentence does more work than the plan.
elaborative_interrogation: Asking why it works is how it stops being a rule and starts being yours.
You interrogated it instead of accepting it. That's the version that sticks.
prospective_regret: Looking at the cost before you pay it is how you stop paying it.
You just made the future consequence present. That's the hard part.
mental_contrasting: That's mental contrasting. Most people skip straight to the plan and wonder why it fails.
Wanting it and naming what's in the way, in the same breath. That's the mechanism.
anchoring: You anchored it to something that already happens. Habits that ride existing ones survive.
Attaching it to a fixed point is why it will still be there in a month.
self_efficacy: You just recorded evidence that you can. Read that back on a bad week.
That's not confidence, it's proof. Different thing, more durable.
attribution: You gave the credit to something you control. That's the attribution that compounds.
How you explain a good night decides whether you can repeat it.
commitment: Written down is a different commitment from thought about. You know this.
That's on the record now. Which was the point.
episodic_future_thinking: You just made tomorrow concrete enough to plan for. Vague futures don't get honoured.
Rehearsing it is most of the work. The rest is showing up.
subtraction: Taking something away is harder than adding, and it holds better.
You removed instead of adding. That's the rarer instinct.
minimum_viable: The smallest version you'll actually do beats the best one you won't.
You shrank it until it was inevitable. Correct move.

identity: Logged. That's the kind of thing that separates people who track from people who intend to.
In the record. You're building a case file on yourself.
Got it. Another night you showed up for this.
Noted. The consistency is the asset, not any single entry.
Down. You keep doing this on the nights it would be easy not to.
Filed. This is what the good version of you does at this hour.
Saved. Most people quit tracking in week two. You're past that.
Recorded. That's one more data point nobody else has on you.
Kept. You're the person who writes it down. That's not nothing.
In. The habit is the point; the entry is just the evidence.
Logged. Doing this tired is worth more than doing it fresh.
Held. Every one of these makes the coaching sharper.
short: Taken. Even the brief ones keep the chain intact.
Logged. A line is enough on a night like this.
Got it. Showing up beats writing well.
In. Brief is fine — missing is the only failure.

milestone.3: Three in a row. That's the point where it stops being a decision each time.
milestone.7: A full week, every night. Most tracking habits die before here.
milestone.14: Fourteen consecutive. Two weeks is where the baseline starts being worth trusting.
milestone.21: Twenty-one straight. You've written more about your sleep this month than most people do in a life.
milestone.30: Thirty nights unbroken. That's a month of evidence about who you are.
milestone.50: Fifty in a row. This isn't a streak any more, it's just what you do.
milestone.100: One hundred consecutive nights. Sit with that one for a second.
